subject: Plugin4Shell: two of four AI agents still unpatched
bodyMarkdown:
If you or anyone on your team runs an AI coding agent, this is the morning to check which version you are on. Two of the four big ones were fixed last week, and the other two were not.

## How a pinned plugin stopped being pinned

Last Thursday the security firm AIR published a flaw it calls Plugin4Shell, and The Register wrote it up the same day. The idea fits in a sentence. Coding agents install plugins by locking them to a 40 character commit hash, a practice called **SHA pinning**, which is supposed to guarantee you get the exact version of the code somebody actually read. The agents ran a git checkout on that hash and then never verified that the files coming back matched it. Git resolves a branch name ahead of a commit hash, so whoever owns the plugin repository can create a branch named after the pinned hash and serve whatever they like. Claude Code and Codex re-run that checkout during background auto-updates, which is what makes the attack **zero-click**, meaning nobody has to install or approve anything for the swap to land.

## Two vendors fixed it, two did not

Help Net Security reported on Friday that two of the four agents are still unpatched. Anthropic fixed Claude Code in version 2.1.179 and OpenAI fixed Codex in 0.146.0, both after AIR's disclosure, which The Hacker News said reached the vendors back in June. Google is not fixing Gemini CLI at all, since it has deprecated the tool and is pointing people to Antigravity, so an install that stays put stays exposed. Microsoft has shipped nothing for Copilot. A GitHub spokesperson said GitHub does not allow branch or tag names that resemble commit SHAs, which does close the hole for plugins hosted there. The researchers' reply is the part I would sit with: Copilot also installs plugins from marketplaces on Bitbucket and on company-run git servers, and those hosts will take a branch named like a hash without complaint.

## The cheap fix nobody wrote

Checking that the hash you asked for is the hash you received is a few lines of code. Four teams with enormous budgets and real security staff all skipped it, the same way, in the same year. I read that as the plugin layer getting built at the speed of the product race, with the review running at that speed too. That worries me, because a plugin runs with the permissions of the developer who launched the agent, which in practice means the source tree, the cloud credentials, the SSH keys and whatever else is sitting in that shell. Enterprise buyers were sold pinning as the control that made agents safe to switch on. Last week the control turned out to be a label on a box.

## The takeaway

Update Claude Code to 2.1.179 and Codex to 0.146.0 this morning, which takes about two minutes. If your team runs Copilot or Gemini CLI with plugins that live anywhere other than GitHub, I would pull those plugins until Microsoft publishes something, because Friday's Help Net Security piece said two of the four remain unpatched and I have not seen an advisory since. Go find out where your plugins are actually hosted, since the whole trick depends on the git host allowing a branch named like a commit hash. I will be watching for a Microsoft advisory, and for the first report of this being used on somebody real rather than in a lab.
